extracted.intended_audience: novelists, creative-writing students, and critics studying narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on choosing and handling narrative method in the novel: pictorial (summary/omniscient) vs dramatic (scenic/enactment), how to account for the narrator's presence, and when to use first-person narration or dramatization to authenticate the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator’s relation to the story / point-of-view accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel must account for 'the question of the narrator’s relation to the story'—who is disposing the scattered facts and whose is this point of view; if the mind that knows the story and the eye that sees it remain unaccountable the book is weakened.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the narrator’s perspective recognizable and verifiable within the book so the reader can measure the line of sight and not feel the author hovering in a void. Methods include dramatising the seeing eye, including the narrator explicitly in the narrative, or otherwise making the point of view an object within the story. Examples and contrasts: Thackeray’s conspicuous omniscience vs. Flaubert’s subtler blend with a character’s perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial (narrative/summary) versus dramatic enactment (scene)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts of a novel that are not scenic tend toward picture—the reflection of somebody’s mind—and parts that need intensity or emphasis give way to enacted drama (scenes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pictorial summary to sweep over wide ranges of life and many facts quickly; reserve dramatic enactment for moments of intensity, climax, or where vivid immediacy is required. Understand that each method has advantages (scope vs. intensity) and costs (loss of intensity vs. loss of breadth). Examples: Thackeray’s panorama for breadth, dramatisation for climactic moments as in Bovary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of dramatic scenes (hoard the novelist’s drama)
rubrics_metrics.description: Drama is 'the novelist’s highest light'—using it prodigally where not needed lessens its force where it is essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overusing scenes; reserve scenic enactment for important occasions so that when a dramatic scene appears it carries weight. The economical procedure is to hoard dramatic treatment rather than to scatter it gratuitously. Example guidance: Bovary’s selective use of scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize the narrator / make the point of view a fact in the story
rubrics_metrics.description: The only way to silence questions about the narrator’s authority is 'somehow to make the mind and the eye objective, to make them facts in the story.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the narrator’s act of recollection or observation as action—a 'play within a play'—so the reader sees who is seeing and from where. Devices include first-person narration by a character in the book (Esmond), or otherwise embedding the narrator as a recognizable presence whose vantage point can be tested by the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of first-person narration (advantages and limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: First-person narration substitutes a characterized 'I' for the loose 'I' of the author, giving precision, individuality, a delimited field of vision, and a meaningful tone, but it has limits when the narrator must both report and be the principal subject of the portrait.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first person when you want a definite bounding line to the picture, a personal tone integrated into the story, or unity for a long retrospective. But beware when the book’s main subject is the narrator’s own inner development: the first-person reporter can vividly recount events but cannot always dramatize the narrator’s inner life as effectively as scenic enactment would. Examples: Advantages—Esmond, David Copperfield; Limits—Meredith’s Harry Richmond, where the narrator is required to be both observer and fully enacted subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person narration for compositional unity (autobiographical shape)
rubrics_metrics.description: The first person can 'compose of its own accord' and give unity to a rambling or retrospective design; 'autobiography... its natural right is to seem wayward and inconsequent; its charm is in the fidelity with which it follows the winding course of the writer’s thought.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the design is essentially a long glance or chronicle of years (a memory-shaped book), first-person narration is particularly useful to bind disparate incidents into a single whole; formlessness can be an asset where fidelity to the narrator’s recollection is desired. Example: David Copperfield.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize inner consciousness when it is the central subject
rubrics_metrics.description: If the book’s primary aim is to show 'what it was like to be' a particular person (the narrator or protagonist), mere reporting is insufficient; the inner history must be made immediate and visible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the subject is psychological or moral development, prefer methods that allow the reader to judge and experience the inner change (scenic enactment, scenes that show effect rather than only an account). Relying solely on a narrator’s retrospective report risks losing conviction about inner transformation. Example problem: Meredith’s Harry Richmond—hero cannot both report and be fully dramatized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine methods to correct each other’s weaknesses
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘Method... can be imposed upon method, one kind upon another’; novelists often correct the weakness of one method by the force of another while retaining advantages of both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t treat pictorial and dramatic methods as exclusive—blend them: dramatize portions of the pictorial narrative, embed scenes within summaries, or dramatize the narrator to give objectivity to summaries. Study how Flaubert blends his acuter vision with a character’s vision to avoid intrusive omniscience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conspicuous authorial intrusion unless justified by the author’s voice
rubrics_metrics.description: A conspicuous omniscient author can leave an 'inconclusive look' or an 'air of ineffectiveness' if the author’s presence is unaccounted for; this thinness grows on re-reading unless the author’s personality fully justifies the intrusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the author insists on omniscience, provide reasons within the fiction for that presence (make it a character, ensure the voice has authority or charm), or reduce intrusion by shifting to an embedded narrator or dramatizing the point of view. Examples: Thackeray’s conspicuous authorial voice contrasted with Flaubert’s unobtrusive intervention; Turgenev’s communicative narrator whose presence sometimes lessens the picture’s authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat scenes with care; avoid neglect and waste
rubrics_metrics.description: The possibilities of the scene are often abused: 'the treatment of the scene is neglected, and yet it recurs again and again, much too often, and its value is wasted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you use dramatic scenes, handle them with craft—scene construction, dialogue, stage direction, and implication—so their repeated appearance does not dilute their effect. Use scenes purposefully (to dramatize inner change, enact crucial conflicts) rather than habitually.
